claims.text: The initially processed high-entropy alloy is a homogeneous, single-phase solid solution.
Rapid solidification followed by high-temperature solution treatment removes segregation and produces the single-phase state.
Thermal-mechanical aging under service-like conditions induces strain-assisted nano-precipitation or phase decomposition.
Elevated temperatures of approximately 300–500°C provide sufficient thermal activation for diffusion in the unspecified alloy.
Stress-assisted diffusion and local compositional fluctuations cause nucleation and growth of a second phase.
The second-phase nanoscale precipitates are brittle.
Nanoscale precipitates or local compositional heterogeneities act as internal stress concentrators and crack-nucleation sites.
The precipitates interrupt otherwise uniform plastic-deformation pathways in the original single-phase alloy.
Precipitate-induced disruption of plastic deformation reduces toughness and promotes brittle fracture.
The as-solution-treated baseline alloy has high toughness and fractures by a ductile mechanism.
Aged specimens will have lower fracture toughness than as-solution-treated specimens.
Aging will shift fracture morphology from microvoid coalescence to cleavage or intergranular cracking.
Sustained elevated temperature and mechanical loading accelerate diffusion and stress-assisted phase separation.
At temperatures well below the activation range, such as room temperature, the proposed phase-separation embrittlement mechanism may not activate.
Very low strain rates are outside the conditions expected to activate the proposed embrittlement mechanism.
The onset temperature, relevant strain-rate thresholds, and magnitude of toughness loss depend on alloy composition and processing history.
